title: Sometimes it's hard
hook: some meditators have difficult experiences, and stopping or getting help is fine (Britton et al., 2017)

segments.voice: Yesterday: what it doesn't show, small studies and big headlines. Your line was no magic. Did you meet a big claim, and ask how big the study was? Day three hundred seven.

Most of what gets said about meditation is some version of: it's calming. And for many people, much of the time, it is. But some people sit down to breathe and something else comes up. Old memories they didn't ask for. A wave of fear. A strange feeling that the world isn't quite real, or that they aren't. Often they tell no one, because everything they've read says this should feel peaceful, so they assume they're doing it wrong. A team of researchers decided to take those people seriously. Today: sometimes it's hard.
screen: `IT'S CALMING, MOSTLY.` → `SOMETHING ELSE COMES UP.` → `THEY TELL NO ONE.`

segments.voice: In 2017 a team at Brown University, led by Jared Lindahl with Willoughby Britton as senior researcher, published a study in the journal PLoS ONE called The varieties of contemplative experience. They interviewed practitioners in Western Buddhist communities who had met difficulties in meditation, and meditation teachers who had seen them in students. They weren't counting how common these experiences are; they were mapping what they're like. They found a wide range. Fear, anxiety and panic. Old trauma resurfacing. Trouble sleeping. Being oversensitive to light or sound. Changes in the sense of self. Some passed in days. Some lasted much longer and affected people's work and relationships. Here's what makes this honest rather than frightening. Many contemplative traditions have known this for centuries. Buddhist, Christian and Sufi teachers have long described hard passages in practice, and that's one reason they insisted on teachers and community rather than sitting alone with a book. The study's point wasn't that meditation is dangerous for everyone. It was that difficulties are real, they're not a sign you're failing, and people deserve to hear about them in advance. So here is the plain guidance this path will always follow. If a practice feels wrong, you can stop. Open your eyes. Feel your feet on the floor. Move, walk, drink some water, talk to someone. Choose a gentler practice, or none for a while. If something lingers, talk to an experienced teacher, a doctor or a therapist, especially if you have a history of trauma. And if you're ever in crisis, reach out to emergency help right away. Stopping is not failing. It's wisdom.
screen: `THE VARIETIES OF CONTEMPLATIVE EXPERIENCE.` · `FEAR, OLD MEMORIES, A CHANGED SELF.` · `TRADITIONS KNEW, AND KEPT TEACHERS.` · `STOP, GROUND, TALK TO SOMEONE.` · then, large: `IT'S OKAY TO STOP.`

segments.voice: Today's sit is about safety. Keep your eyes open, softly. Feel your feet on the floor and your weight in the chair. Name three things you can see. Breathe normally. Know that at any moment during these two minutes you can stand up, stretch, or stop, and that would be exactly right. Just rest here, grounded. The bell holds the time.
Sometimes it's hard. Some meditators meet real difficulties, and stopping, grounding or getting help is always fine. Today's word.
Your line: it's okay to stop. If any practice, here or anywhere, feels wrong, stop it and ground yourself, and tell someone. Day three hundred seven.

howItsDone: Experienced meditation teachers watch for difficult experiences in students, suggest grounding and gentler practices, and refer people to clinicians when difficulties persist.

sources.ref: Lindahl, Fisher, Cooper, Rosen and Britton, 'The varieties of contemplative experience', PLoS ONE 12(5):e0176239 (2017)

notes: The outline cites 'Britton et al., 2017'; the paper's first author is Jared Lindahl, with Willoughby Britton as senior author. The script names both.
Study details: about 60 practitioners and 32 teachers interviewed; 59 categories across 7 domains; confirm figures before adding any.

Safety guidance (stop, ground, seek a teacher, doctor or therapist; emergency help in crisis) is general and intentionally not clinical advice; a clinician reviewer may want to check wording, and the app's crisis card should be reachable from this day.
